about.metaDescription: What IdeaNest is, how all-or-nothing funding works, and what it costs.
about.title: About IdeaNest
about.summary: A place to fund things that do not exist yet, on terms that are the same for everybody.
about.intro: IdeaNest is a reward-based crowdfunding platform. A creator publishes a campaign with a goal and a deadline; people who want the thing to exist pledge towards it; and if the goal is met by the deadline, the pledges are collected and the creator makes the thing. If it is not, nobody is charged at all.

allOrNothing.heading: All or nothing, and why it is not a detail
allOrNothing.first: A partly funded campaign is worse than an unfunded one. It leaves a creator holding money that is not enough to finish with and backers holding a promise nobody can keep. So a campaign that misses its goal collects nothing, costs its creator no fee, and leaves every card untouched.
allOrNothing.second: The consequence is that a deadline means something. A campaign at 90% on its last day is genuinely at risk, and the platform says so rather than dressing it up.

cost.heading: What it costs
cost.successful: A successful campaign pays 5% of what it raised, plus the payment processor’s own fee — roughly 2.5–3% and a small fixed amount per pledge.
cost.unsuccessful: An unsuccessful campaign pays nothing. No listing fee, no platform fee, no processing fee.
cost.note: Rates are configuration rather than code, so a category or an individual agreement can carry a different one. The rate above is the standard schedule.

notAPurchase.heading: A pledge is not a purchase
notAPurchase.body: This is the sentence most worth reading twice. Backing a campaign funds an attempt. The creator is accountable for the attempt and for telling backers honestly how it is going; they are not a shop with the thing in a warehouse. Every campaign has to publish its risks and challenges before it can be submitted, and that section is required rather than encouraged.

next.heading: Where to go next
next.body: <howItWorks>How it works</howItWorks> walks through backing and running a campaign step by step. <trustSafety>Trust and safety</trustSafety> covers review, reporting, and what happens to your data.

howItWorks.metaDescription: Backing a campaign, running one, and what happens between a pledge and a parcel on IdeaNest.
howItWorks.title: How it works
howItWorks.summary: What happens between finding a campaign and holding the thing it funded.

backing.heading: If you are backing something
backing.first: Choose a reward tier, or pledge without one. Your card is authorised and nothing is taken while the campaign is running — you can change your pledge, move to a different tier, add an extra, or cancel outright until the deadline.
backing.second: At the deadline one of two things happens. If the campaign reached its goal, every confirmed pledge is collected and the campaign moves into fulfilment. If it did not, nothing is collected, no fee is charged, and the stored card tokens are deleted within thirty days.
backing.third: A card can fail at collection — expired, out of funds, refused by a bank. There is a seven-day window in which it is retried before the pledge is given up on.

surveys.heading: Then the creator asks you some questions
surveys.first: Most rewards need something the campaign page cannot know: a size, a colour, an edition, and somewhere to send it. That arrives as a survey, and it appears under <surveys>surveys</surveys> in your account. Your shipping address is held separately from your answers and encrypted at rest, and it belongs to the pledge rather than to your account — so two campaigns can go to two different places.
surveys.second: As parcels go out, <deliveries>deliveries</deliveries> shows the carrier and the tracking number for each one.

running.heading: If you are running a campaign
running.draft: Draft it. A title, a summary, a category, a goal, a duration between one and sixty days, and a cover image. The story needs at least 500 characters and the risks section at least 200 — both are required.
running.rewards: Add rewards. Up to a hundred tiers, each with a price, what is in it, and where it ships. A tier’s price cannot change once the campaign is live, and a tier with backers cannot be deleted — only hidden.
running.submit: Submit it for review. A person reads it. They approve it, ask for changes, or reject it with a reason.
running.launch: Launch. From this point the goal and the deadline are fixed. Everything else — the story, the updates, the reward quantities upwards — stays editable.
running.deliver: Deliver. Send the survey, collect the addresses, lock them when you start printing labels, and record tracking as parcels go out.

agreeing.heading: What you are agreeing to as a backer
agreeing.first: A pledge funds an attempt rather than buying a finished object. The creator owes you an honest account of how it is going — that is what campaign updates are for — and the platform owes you the tools to see it and to report a campaign that is not being honest. Neither of those is the same as a guarantee that the thing will arrive.
agreeing.second: <trustSafety>Trust and safety</trustSafety> sets out what is checked, and what to do when something is wrong.

trustSafety.metaDescription: How campaigns are reviewed, what is not allowed, how to report something, and what happens to your money and your data.
trustSafety.title: Trust and safety
trustSafety.summary: What is checked, what is not, and what to do when something looks wrong.

review.heading: Every campaign is read before it goes live
review.first: A campaign cannot publish itself. It is submitted, a person reviews it against the rules below, and it is approved, sent back for changes, or rejected with a reason. Nothing on the platform reaches the public without passing through that.
review.second: Review is not verification. A reviewer checks that a campaign is what it says it is, is allowed to be funded, and is not somebody else’s work. They are not in a position to confirm that a creator can manufacture what they have drawn — which is why a pledge is described everywhere on this platform as funding an attempt.

notAllowed.heading: What is not allowed
notAllowed.prohibited: Prohibited items — things the platform does not allow to be funded at all.
notAllowed.misrepresentation: Misrepresentation — a campaign that states something untrue about itself.
notAllowed.notOwn: Work that is not the creator’s own, or that uses somebody else’s intellectual property.
notAllowed.offensive: Offensive material, and content that targets people for who they are.
notAllowed.spam: Spam, and campaigns that exist to advertise something else.
notAllowed.fraud: Fraud — where there is reason to believe nobody intends to deliver.

reporting.heading: Reporting something
reporting.first: A campaign, a comment or an account can be reported by anybody with an IdeaNest account. A report goes to a moderator, not to an automatic filter: nothing disappears because five people objected to it, and a report is a request for a person to look.
reporting.second: Reporting the same thing twice does not add weight — the second report returns the first one. Reports are not public, and the account being reported is not told who reported it.

money.heading: Your money
money.first: Card details never reach IdeaNest’s own servers; payments go through the provider’s hosted fields. While a campaign is running your pledge is an authorisation rather than a charge, and a campaign that misses its goal takes nothing at all.
money.second: Every payment operation is idempotent, which is the unglamorous property that matters most: a request that is retried because a connection dropped produces one pledge and one charge, not two.

account.heading: Your account and your data
account.twoFactor: Two-factor authentication is available on every account and required before a payout. Set it up under two-factor authentication.
account.devices: Every signed-in device is listed under devices, and any of them can be signed out from any other.
account.addresses: Shipping addresses are encrypted at rest and are visible to a creator only for the campaign you backed.
account.data: A copy of your data is a download, and closing your account keeps it for thirty days before anonymising it — so a closure made in anger, or by somebody else, can be undone. Both are under data and closure.

limits.heading: What we cannot do
limits.first: IdeaNest cannot make a campaign deliver. What it can do is keep the record honest: a campaign’s updates, its comments and the way to report it are all on the campaign’s own page, where somebody deciding whether to back it will see them.
limits.second: A creator can moderate comments on their own campaign, and a removed one does not vanish — the row stays, marked as removed. A comment thread that has been cleaned out therefore still looks like one, which is the point: a page with nothing on it and a page with twelve removals are different things, and a reader is entitled to tell them apart.
